key_terms.meaning: A fixed-length vector x (for example an averaged word-vector) goes through dense layers, h = relu(Wx + b), then a softmax over class labels.
A filter of width w slides along the word-vector sequence and outputs a score at each position; max-pooling keeps the strongest score per filter.
w is the number of consecutive tokens the convolution filter looks at in one step; w = 3 scores three-word phrases such as 'not very good'.
The vector an RNN carries forward after reading token t: h_t = tanh(W_h h_(t−1) + W_x x_t + b).
Input, forget and output gates with values in (0,1) decide what to write into, keep in, and read out of the cell state c_t, which is the long-term memory.
A gated recurrent unit with two gates (update and reset) and no separate cell state; cheaper than LSTM and often similar in accuracy.
One network reads the source sentence into states, a second network generates the target sentence, so input and output lengths can differ.
The decoder scores every encoder state, turns the scores into weights that sum to 1, and uses the weighted average as its context vector.
During seq2seq training the decoder is fed the true previous target token instead of its own prediction, which speeds up and stabilises learning.
Each position forms a query, key and value; scores are softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k), and every position mixes information from all other positions in one parallel step.
Several self-attention heads run in parallel on projected query, key and value subspaces, and their outputs are concatenated and projected.
A vector added to each token embedding so the transformer, which has no built-in order, knows where each token sits in the sequence.
BERT's pretraining task: hide about 15% of tokens and train the model to predict them from both left and right context.
After pretraining, the whole network is trained a little more on a small labelled task, usually with a new task-specific output head.
The rule that picks the next token: greedy, beam search, temperature scaling, top-k or nucleus (top-p) sampling.
Bilingual Evaluation Understudy: a score from 0 to 1 built from clipped n-gram precision of the output against reference translations, multiplied by a brevity penalty.
Given a premise and a hypothesis, classify the pair as entailment, contradiction or neutral.
The model predicts a start index and an end index inside the passage; the answer is the text between them.
A classic ranking function that scores a document for a query using term frequency, inverse document frequency and document length normalisation.
Ranking documents in one language for a query in another, usually by mapping both into a shared embedding space or by translating the query first.

takeaways: A text classifier only needs a fixed-size vector, but a 1D convolution can learn which local word patterns matter instead of treating the vector as a bag.
A recurrent network is the simplest way to make word order matter, because the hidden state is a running summary of everything read so far.
Gates in LSTM and GRU let the network keep useful information for many steps and drop the rest, which fights the vanishing gradient.
Attention removes the bottleneck of squeezing a whole sentence into one vector, and it is the idea that made transformers possible.
Self-attention compares every position with every other position in parallel, which is why transformers train faster on GPUs than RNNs.
Pretraining on unlabelled text teaches general language; fine-tuning on a few thousand labelled examples adapts it to the actual task.
A decoder-only large language model is just a next-token predictor; the decoding rule decides whether the output is safe and repetitive or creative and risky.
BLEU compares surface n-grams, so it rewards overlap with references and can miss a correct paraphrase.
Question answering and textual entailment are both sentence-pair classification once the text is tokenised into one joint input.
Retrieval and generation are usually combined: find the right documents first, then let the model read them, instead of trusting its memory.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to move from the architecture diagram to the equations to a named NLP application, and to show why the design choice (convolution, recurrence, attention) fixes a stated weakness of the earlier model.

bank.q: Explain a feedforward neural network model for text classification. Draw the architecture, write the layer equations, and contrast it with a 1D CNN model for the same task.
outline: Input is a fixed-length vector: averaged or concatenated word embeddings, or a bag-of-words vector
Dense layer h = relu(Wx + b), then softmax output over classes
Loss is cross-entropy; trained by backpropagation with a gradient-descent variant
1D CNN: filter of width w slides over the token sequence, produces a feature map, max-pooling keeps the strongest score
CNN keeps local word order inside the window w, the feedforward model does not
CNN shares weights across positions, so it sees n-grams it never saw at a fixed input position

bank.q: Describe RNN, LSTM and GRU sequence models. Explain each gate in LSTM and state clearly how gating addresses the vanishing gradient problem.
outline: RNN recurrence h_t = tanh(W_h h_(t−1) + W_x x_t + b) and the same weights at every step
Problem: repeated multiplication through many steps makes gradients shrink or blow up
LSTM cell state c_t updated additively; forget gate f_t, input gate i_t, output gate o_t
GRU: update gate and reset gate, single state, fewer parameters
Additive cell-state path gives gradients a short route back through time
Use cases: POS tagging, NER, sentiment over a review

bank.q: Explain the encoder-decoder (seq2seq) model with attention. Why is a single fixed context vector a bottleneck, and how does attention fix it?
outline: Encoder RNN reads the source and returns states h_1 ... h_T
Decoder generates one target token per step, conditioned on its previous token and a context vector
Fixed vector must compress the whole sentence, especially weak for long sentences
Attention: score each encoder state against the decoder state, softmax to weights that sum to 1, weighted sum as context
Weights can be inspected and align source and target words
Teacher forcing during training, free-running generation at inference

bank.q: Explain self-attention and multi-head attention in the transformer. Write the scaled dot-product formula and compare BERT with GPT in architecture, pretraining objective and typical use.
outline: Query, key, value projections from each token embedding
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V, scaling stops softmax saturation
Multiple heads learn different relations; concatenate and project
Add positional encoding, residual connection and layer normalisation, feedforward block
BERT: encoder-only, masked language modelling plus next-sentence prediction, good for classification and span QA
GPT: decoder-only, causal next-token prediction, good for generation
Both are pretrained then fine-tuned

bank.q: Define BLEU. Write its formula, explain clipped n-gram precision and the brevity penalty, and state two limitations of the metric.
outline: BLEU = brevity penalty × exp(mean of log p_n) for n = 1 to N, usually N = 4
p_n = clipped matching n-grams divided by total candidate n-grams
Clipping stops a repeated word from inflating precision
Brevity penalty = 1 if candidate length ≥ reference length, else exp(1 − r/c)
Range 0 to 1, often reported as a percentage
Limits: ignores meaning and paraphrase, weak on morphology-rich languages, depends on reference set

bank.q: A decoder has two encoder states with scores 2, 1 and 0 before softmax. Compute the attention weights and the context vector when the state vectors are [1, 0], [0, 1] and [1, 1]. Show every step.
outline: Exponentiate: e², e¹, e⁰ giving about 7.39, 2.72, 1.00
Result about [0.755, 0.335]
State that weights sum to 1 and the largest score dominates
Note that scaling by √d_k keeps such scores moderate

bank.q: Design and train a sentiment classifier for code-mixed Hindi-English tweets. Choose an architecture from this unit, describe preprocessing, input representation, training and evaluation.
outline: Preprocessing: normalise casing, handle emoji and hashtags, keep negations
Tokenisation robust to code-mixing; subword units help with misspellings
Representation: pretrained multilingual embeddings or a multilingual transformer
Model choice with reasoning: fine-tuned BERT-style encoder or CNN over embeddings
Class imbalance handling, train/validation/test split, cross-entropy loss
Metrics: accuracy, macro F1, confusion matrix; error analysis on sarcasm and negation

bank.q: You must build an extractive question answering system over a large collection of exam notes. Describe how a BERT-style span model produces an answer and how Exact Match and F1 are computed for evaluation.
outline: Retrieve candidate passages first, then run the reader model on each
Input format: [CLS] question [SEP] passage [SEP] with segment embeddings
Two output heads score every passage token as start and as end; softmax over positions
Take the highest scoring valid span with start ≤ end
Exact Match: 1 if the predicted string equals a reference answer after normalisation, else 0
F1: token overlap between prediction and reference; report max over reference answers and average over the set
No-answer handling with a threshold on the [CLS] score

bank.q: A user types a Tamil query and the document collection is in English. Explain, with a block diagram, how you would build a cross-lingual retrieval system and how you would evaluate it.
outline: Option 1: translate the query to English, then run monolingual retrieval
Option 2: map query and documents into one multilingual embedding space and use nearest neighbours
Option 3: translate documents offline, or use a bilingual dictionary for query expansion
Indexing with inverted index and BM25 as a strong baseline; dense retrieval as an alternative
Evaluation with pooled relevance judgements and measures such as precision at k, recall and mean average precision
Report per-language results; watch for translation errors and named entities

bank.q: Compare CNN, RNN/LSTM and transformer encoders for classifying long documents. Discuss long-range dependencies, parallelism, parameter count and training cost, and recommend one for a specific case.
outline: CNN: local window w, parallel, cheap, needs stacked layers or dilation for long range
RNN: sequential, cannot parallelise over time, hidden state drifts over hundreds of tokens
Transformer: every pair of positions interacts in one step but cost grows with the square of sequence length
Memory and GPU utilisation compared; truncated or chunked input for long documents
Pretrained transformer usually wins with limited labelled data; CNN or simple model wins with small data and tight compute
Recommendation must be justified against the stated constraints

bank.q: Large language models sometimes produce fluent but false statements. Analyse the causes, propose evaluation methods, and discuss mitigations including retrieval augmentation and instruction tuning.
outline: Cause: the model predicts likely tokens, it is not a database lookup; pretraining data noise and gaps
Decoding amplifies errors because each wrong token conditions the next
Evaluation: human factuality rating, task accuracy, exact match against gold answers, adversarial question sets
Mitigation: retrieval-augmented generation, citation of sources, instruction and preference tuning, lower temperature, abstain option
Residual risk remains; systems need human review for high-stakes use
Discuss cost and latency trade-off

bank.q: Evaluate BLEU as the main metric for a machine translation system used in Indian language news translation. Suggest what you would report alongside it.
outline: BLEU is precision-based on surface n-grams against one or more references
Multiple references help but coverage of paraphrases is incomplete
Weak for free word order and rich morphology; tokenisation choice changes the score
Add chrF or METEOR for character and recall balance; add COMET-style learned metrics if available
Add human adequacy and fluency ratings on a sample
Report per-language pairs, and add a domain-specific terminology check

bank.q: Compare an open-domain generative question answering system with a retrieve-then-read pipeline. Discuss accuracy, cost, latency, controllability and hallucination.
outline: Generative: fluent and flexible, can answer without an explicit passage, but may fabricate
Retrieve-then-read: answer grounded in a passage, span is checkable, but limited by retrieval recall
Cost and latency of retrieval plus reader versus one large model call
Controllability: the retrieve-then-read output can be verified against the source
Hybrid: retrieve, then let a language model summarise the retrieved passages with citations
Discuss evaluation: exact match and F1 favour extractive; human rating needed for generative

bank.q: Explain how the same transformer encoder can be fine-tuned for sentiment analysis, textual entailment and span-based question answering. What changes and what stays fixed?
outline: Shared pretrained body: embeddings, self-attention layers, feedforward blocks
Sentiment: [CLS] vector into a linear layer with softmax over classes
Entailment: premise and hypothesis concatenated with [SEP] and segment embeddings, [CLS] into a three-way classifier
Span QA: two linear heads over token positions for start and end
Change the head and the data; the pretrained weights are updated slightly with a small learning rate
Same pretraining objective explains why one model transfers to three tasks

glossary.def: The unit of text a model reads, usually a word or a subword piece produced by a tokeniser.
A dense vector of real numbers representing a word, subword or sentence.
Splitting rare words into frequent pieces so the model can handle unseen words, as in byte-pair encoding.
A method that learns word vectors by predicting a word from its neighbours, or its neighbours from the word.
A function that turns a vector of scores into positive weights that sum to 1.
The negative log probability the model gives to the correct class; the standard training objective for classification.
Taking the largest value over positions in a feature map, keeping the strongest evidence for a pattern.
The shrinking of gradients as they are backpropagated through many steps, which stops early layers from learning.
The long-term memory vector inside an LSTM, updated additively through gates.
Decoding that keeps the k best partial sequences at each step instead of only the single best.
Three learned projections of each token used to compute attention scores and the weighted output.
The vector the decoder uses at a step, formed as a weighted sum of encoder states under attention.
A mask that blocks attention to future positions so a decoder-only model can only look left.
Training a model on a large unlabelled corpus with a self-supervised objective before any task-specific training.
Further training a language model on instruction and response pairs so it follows user requests.
A number that divides the logits before softmax; low values make output focused, high values make it random.
The softmax output over the vocabulary at one decoding step, from which the next token is chosen.
A human-written target sentence used as the gold standard when scoring machine translation output.
In natural language inference, the sentence that is assumed true and must be checked against the hypothesis.
In natural language inference, the sentence whose truth is judged relative to the premise.
The label used when the hypothesis cannot be true given the premise.
The label used when the premise neither supports nor contradicts the hypothesis.
A lookup from each term to the list of documents containing it, used for fast retrieval.
A human label saying whether a document is relevant to a query, used to score a retrieval system.
